Cardiac fibers are nonstriated and cannot rebuild their filaments
Skeletal muscle is voluntary, and practice regrows its fibers

The muscle that bends your elbow

The muscles that move your eyes

Cardiac muscle tissue
Smooth muscle tissue

Pushing needs more ATP than muscle can supply
It relaxes completely whenever the arm is bent
A shortening fiber can pull but not push

Stem cells beside it pushed their nuclei into it after birth

Glial cells and muscle fibers
Nerves and axons

The axon terminals
The dendrites
The nucleus

Away from the cell body toward the axon terminals
From the axon terminals back to the cell body
In either direction, depending on where the signal starts

The cell body combines the incoming signals
The axon carries a signal away from the cell body

options: The axon
The dendrites
The axon terminals
The cell body

The cut destroyed the neurons' cell bodies in his wrist

The cell body and dendrites of one neuron
A bundle of many axons wrapped in connective tissue
A cluster of glial cells packed together inside the brain

q: Which of these are jobs of glial cells? Select all that apply.

Carrying long-distance signals from the spinal cord to the toes
Controlling the makeup of the fluid around neurons
Engulfing dead cells and microbes
Holding neurons in place

q: A 45-year-old woman has a cancerous tumor that began in her brain tissue. From which cells did it most likely grow?
options: Neurons
Fibroblasts
Nerves
Glial cells

q: This description of how a signal passes through a neuron contains one wrong step. Find it.
options: Dendrites receive signals from other neurons
The cell body combines the incoming signals
The axon carries the signal toward the cell body
Axon terminals release chemicals by exocytosis
The next cell responds to the chemicals

q: Fill in the missing step. An axon is cut in the forearm → ______ → the part of the axon beyond the cut breaks down within days.

That part takes in a new nucleus from the glial cells nearby
Blood floods into the axon and dissolves it
The cell body releases chemicals that dissolve it

q: A man's heart stops for six minutes before it is restarted. His heart muscle and skin recover, but he has lasting brain damage. Which features of neurons best explain why they were hurt most?

They are avascular and depend on diffusion

Divide more often
Release chemicals from the tips of its dendrites
Receive signals from many other neurons

It sends the signal back toward the cell body
It divides to form a new neuron
It holds on to the signal until the neuron is at rest again

q: A disease destroys the glial wrapping around the axons in one region, but leaves the axons themselves intact at first. Predict the effect on each variable for those axons.

Number of axons in the region (at first)
Time for a signal to reach the axon terminals

q: The name dendrite comes from a root that describes its shape. What does dendr- mean?
options: Tree
Axis
Glue
Nerve

Neurons outnumber glial cells about ten to one
The brain has roughly equal numbers of each
The adult brain has no glial cells left

q: A small sample of a nerve from the leg is examined under a microscope. What will it contain?
options: The cell bodies of the neurons whose axons it carries
One very large neuron running the length of the leg
Axons, connective tissue and small blood vessels
Cardiac muscle fibers that move signals along
misconception: a nerve is a single neuron

q: A resting neuron's membrane potential is reported as −70 mV. What does the minus sign tell you?

The outside of the cell is negative compared with the inside
The cell has lost 70 mmol/L of positive ions
The cytosol holds more negative ions than positive ions throughout

q: An experimental cell has a membrane that lets potassium through and no other ion. It starts with 140 mmol/L K+ inside and 4 mmol/L outside. Where does its membrane potential settle?
options: At 0 mV
At about −70 mV, the typical resting value
At about +60 mV
At about −90 mV

q: A typical neuron rests at −70 mV. Potassium's equilibrium potential is about −90 mV and sodium's is about +60 mV. What best explains why the resting value lies so much closer to potassium's?
options: Potassium ions are smaller and lighter than sodium ions
Far more potassium channels are open at rest
Each pump cycle moves more potassium ions than sodium ions
The body contains more total potassium than total sodium

q: Mr. Okafor, 62, with kidney failure, has a blood potassium of 7.1 mmol/L (normal 3.5–5.0). What happens to the resting membrane potential of his heart muscle cells?

It becomes less negative (depolarized)
It becomes positive
misconception: the potassium inside cells is what changes in hyperkalemia

q: Ms. Reyes, 48, takes a water pill that makes her kidneys lose potassium. Her blood potassium is now 2.8 mmol/L. In most of her cells, how does the resting membrane potential change?
options: It becomes more negative
It becomes less negative
It becomes positive
It does not change

q: Which of these make the inside of a resting cell more negative? Select all that apply.
options: Potassium diffusing out through leak channels
Negatively charged proteins that cannot leave the cell
The pump moving 3 Na+ out for every 2 K+ in
Sodium diffusing in through leak channels
Water entering the cell by osmosis

q: A neuron's membrane potential moves from −70 mV to −60 mV. The inside is still negative. What is this change called?
options: Hyperpolarization
Repolarization
Depolarization
Reversal of polarity
misconception: depolarization means the inside becomes positive

q: A neuron at rest opens extra potassium channels, and its membrane potential moves from −70 mV to −78 mV. Which best explains the change?
options: More potassium enters, neutralizing negative charge inside
More potassium leaves, moving the voltage toward −90 mV
More sodium leaks in, adding positive charge inside
The pump slows, so fewer positive ions are exported

q: After a brief depolarization to +20 mV, a membrane returns to −70 mV. What is the return called?
options: Hyperpolarization
Depolarization
Equilibrium
Repolarization

variables.name: Potassium concentration gradient across the membrane
How negative potassium's equilibrium potential is
How negative the resting membrane potential is

q: Level 4. A toxin completely blocks every sodium–potassium pump in a neuron. Predict each variable first in the first few seconds, then after several hours.

variables.name: How negative the resting potential is, in the first few seconds
Sodium concentration inside the cell, after several hours
Potassium concentration gradient, after several hours
How negative the resting potential is, after several hours

misconception: the pump creates the resting potential

q: Put the events that set up the resting membrane potential in order.
options: The pump builds high potassium inside and high sodium outside
Potassium diffuses out through open leak channels
Negative proteins left behind make the inside negative
The negative inside pulls potassium back, slowing its exit
A small sodium leak settles the voltage near −70 mV

q: One step in this account of the resting potential is wrong. Find it.
options: Potassium is about 140 mmol/L inside and about 4 mmol/L outside

Sodium leaves the cell through leak channels, carrying positive charge out

Sodium rushes in to replace the potassium
The pump moves potassium back in at the same rate
Chloride leaves the cell alongside the potassium

q: A student says: "Building a −70 mV resting potential must drain a large share of the cell's potassium." What is the best response?
options: Correct: about half of the cell's potassium leaves
Correct, which is why the pump must refill the cell after every change in voltage
Incorrect: potassium does not move at rest
Incorrect: far fewer than one potassium ion in a thousand needs to leave
misconception: building the resting potential empties the cell of potassium

q: A resting cell suddenly opens so many sodium channels that it passes sodium far more easily than potassium. Where does its membrane potential head?
options: Toward −90 mV
Toward +60 mV
Toward 0 mV and stops there

q: Which statement best describes the main role of the sodium–potassium pump in a resting cell?

It keeps the ion gradients from running down
It opens potassium leak channels
It moves sodium into the cell

options: −70 mV
0 mV
+70 mV

q: Blood flow to part of a patient's brain stops. Within minutes, neurons in that area lose their resting potential. What is the most direct chain of events?
options: Low oxygen opens sodium leak channels, which flood the cells with sodium
Less ATP is made, the pumps slow, and the gradients run down
Low oxygen blocks potassium leak channels, so no charge separates
Low oxygen raises the potassium concentration inside the neurons

options: A neuron
A skeletal muscle fiber
A heart muscle cell
A red blood cell
A fibroblast in a tendon

q: A light touch depolarizes a nerve ending by 3 mV. A firmer touch at the same spot depolarizes it by 9 mV. Neither reaches threshold. What kind of change is this?

Graded potentials
A refractory period
Hyperpolarization

q: A stimulus depolarizes a neuron's membrane from −70 mV to −60 mV. Threshold is −55 mV. What happens next?

A full action potential, delayed slightly
The depolarization fades and the membrane returns to rest
The membrane stays at −60 mV until another stimulus arrives

q: A sensory nerve fiber fires action potentials that peak at +30 mV when you touch it lightly. You press twice as hard. What changes in the fiber's action potentials?

The membrane reaches about +30 mV
Sodium channels close and potassium flows out through voltage-gated channels
